title: Pauri 1, sound: sochai soch
hookLine: sochai soch na hovaee je sochee lakh vaar
tomorrow: Pauri 1, meaning: the wall of falsehood

cards: Two in the morning, lying awake, going over the same conversation for the fortieth time. Planning what you'll say. Rehearsing.
Turning it over, as if one more lap will settle it. Ever tried to solve a feeling by thinking about it? The first real verse of Japji starts right there, inside the thinking.
And it opens with an almost tongue-twister: the same word twice in a row, like a person pacing a room.

teach.h: PAURI — A STEP ON A LADDER.
teach.b: A pauri is a step, a rung on a ladder. Japji is built from thirty-eight of them, and this is the first.
Its opening line: sochai soch na hovaee, je sochee lakh vaar. Sound it out. Sochai: SO-chai, the ai like the start of hair, but short.
Soch: rhymes, roughly, with coach, softened. Together, sochai soch: the same root twice, back and forth. Na hovaee: na, no; ho-VA-ee.

Je sochee: jay SO-chee. Lakh vaar: lakh is a hundred thousand, the lakh you hear in Indian numbers; vaar is times. The meaning peeks through: soch is thinking, and lakh vaar is a hundred thousand times.
The full meaning comes tomorrow. Today, the sound. Sochai, soch, sochee: three forms of one word in one short line.

teach.h: THE LINE LOOPS LIKE A MIND.
teach.b: It sounds like what it describes, a mind going round and round, and it lands on lakh vaar, a number as tired as a mind at two in the morning. The rest of the pauri keeps the build.
The next line begins chupai chup na hovaee: the same doubling, this time with chup, silence. Then a line about hunger with its own doubling, bhukhiaa bhukh, and then one about cleverness.
Then the pauri stops and asks a question: kiv sachiaaraa hoeeai?
Yesterday's word hides inside it: sach, in sachiaaraa, the one who is true. The last line gives the answer, with a word for tomorrow.

how: The first pauri of Japji is recited each morning right after the opening salok; many Sikhs know it by heart from hearing it daily.

o: a person who keeps ritually clean
a person who has become true
a person who thinks very deeply

games.q: match the sound to its sense.

s: and today is the first step.
the first line uses the word for thinking only once
sochai, soch, sochee: three forms in one line.
the first pauri ends without an answer
it asks how to become true, and the last line answers.

games.q: the first pauri doubles a word in its opening, then does it again in the next line. what's the second doubled word?
games.why: chupai chup na hovaee: the same pacing build, this time with silence.

practice: Walk the line the way a mind walks a room: on one out-breath, sochai soch na hovaee; on the next, je sochee lakh vaar. Three times, slower each time, feeling the loop of soch, soch, sochee.
Then let it go and sit; if your mind starts its own laps, just notice it pacing and let the breath be slower than the thoughts, and if you pray, you can rest in Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Sachiaaraa. The one who is true, the question Japji's first pauri asks after sochai soch, a hundred thousand times of thinking, fails to get there.

carryVoice: Your line: sochai soch. A hundred thousand laps, and the question is still waiting. That's day one hundred sixty-three.
